120.title: The bedtime Shema
120.hook: before sleep: the Shema, and forgiveness for anyone who hurt you that day
120.howItsDone: Before sleep, many Jews say the bedtime Shema: a declaration forgiving anyone who wronged them, the Shema, the Hamapil blessing, and verses such as Psalm 31:6 and the line about the four angels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dayan HaEmet, three words inside grief, then silence. Your line was even here, a word. Today, the last blessing of the day, and the last day of this part of the path.

Late at night, lights off. A tired body, a mind replaying the day. What she said in the meeting. The text he never answered. The driver who cut in. The comeback, rewritten. Midnight, then one. A grudge makes a strange pillow, and plenty of nights end on one. Jewish tradition has a practice for this hour, and its first step is letting go. Today: Modeh Ani, and its bookend.
screen: `THE LIGHTS ARE OFF.` → `REPLAYING THE DAY.` → `ASLEEP, HOLDING A GRUDGE.`

segments.voice: Back in camp one, you learned the Shema, the line at the heart of Jewish prayer. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Jews say the Shema in the evening prayers, and the Talmud says to say it again in bed, right before sleep. It points to a psalm: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." Over the centuries, it grew into a short bedtime service. Many prayer books begin with a declaration: first, a person forgives anyone who angered or hurt them that day, in body, money, honor or anything else, by accident or on purpose, and asks that no one be punished on their account. The Talmud tells of Mar Zutra, a rabbi who did this every night: before bed, he said, I forgive everyone who troubled me. Then the Shema, and a blessing thanking God, who lets sleep fall on my eyes. Many add a psalm: "Into Thy hand I commit my spirit." And in many homes, children and adults say a line about four angels: Michael on my right, Gabriel on my left, Uriel in front, Raphael behind, and above my head, God's presence. Angels came up before, in the Friday-night song of welcome; at bedtime, four are named. See the shape of it. It opens with thank you, Modeh Ani, before your feet touch the floor. It closes with I forgive you, before your eyes close. Blessings all the way through.
screen: `THE SHEMA, AGAIN, IN BED.` · `I FORGIVE ANYONE WHO HURT ME.` · `MAR ZUTRA, EVERY NIGHT.` · `FOUR ANGELS AROUND THE BED.` · then, large: `INTO THY HAND I COMMIT MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Let one small hurt from today or this week come to mind, not the biggest, something you can manage, and picture the person. You don't have to say they were right, or call them; set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor before bed, and say to yourself: I forgive this, for tonight. If you pray, you can hand it to God.
Modeh Ani, the morning thanks said before your feet touch the floor, the bookend to the bedtime Shema's forgiveness before sleep.
Your line: forgive before sleeping. Tomorrow a new part begins: the holidays, starting with the calendar. Day one hundred twenty, and counting.

121.title: The Jewish calendar
121.hook: a lunar year with a leap month seven times in nineteen years, so festivals keep their seasons
121.howItsDone: Jewish communities keep a lunisolar calendar: months follow the moon, a second Adar is added seven times in nineteen years, and each day, Shabbat and festival begins at sunset. Many families keep a printed luach from their synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Modeh Ani, the morning thanks, and bedtime's quiet line forgiving anyone who hurt you. Your line was forgive before sleeping.

Ask a Jewish friend when Hanukkah is this year, and there's a good chance they'll have to look it up. One year it starts in late November. Another year it lands right on top of Christmas. Passover drifts around March and April. Rosh Hashanah can come in early September or in October. It looks like the holidays wander. They don't. They're keeping time, just not by the clock on your phone. For the next few weeks, i'll walk you through the Jewish year, one holiday at a time, as they arrive. First, the thing that holds them all.
screen: `WHEN IS HANUKKAH THIS YEAR?` → `THE HOLIDAYS SEEM TO WANDER.` → `THEY'RE KEEPING A DIFFERENT CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for a calendar is luach: a tablet or a board, the same word used for the tablets Moses carried down the mountain. Today a luach is often a printed calendar on a synagogue wall, or an app. The Jewish calendar runs on the moon. Each month begins at the new moon and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days, the time the moon takes to go from dark to dark. In the first chapter of Genesis, the lights in the sky are made "for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years." The Psalms say it plainly: "Who appointedst the moon for seasons." Here's the problem. Twelve moon months fall about eleven days short of the sun's year. A purely lunar calendar slides backward through the seasons, and the Torah ties Passover to spring and Sukkot to the harvest. So, seven times in every nineteen years, the calendar adds a whole extra month, a second Adar, in late winter. That pulls the moon back in line with the sun, and Passover stays in spring. For centuries, a court in Jerusalem declared each new month when witnesses reported seeing the thin new moon. Later, tradition says in the fourth century, the calendar was fixed by calculation, so Jews scattered around the world could keep the same days. A Jewish day begins at sunset, because Genesis says "there was evening and there was morning." And the years are counted from creation, as the rabbis reckoned it, which is why a Hebrew year number runs into the five thousands.
screen: `LUACH: A TABLET, A CALENDAR.` · `EACH MONTH BEGINS AT THE NEW MOON.` · `A LEAP MONTH, SEVEN TIMES IN NINETEEN.` · `THE DAY BEGINS AT SUNSET.` · then, large: `THE MOON FOR SEASONS.`

segments.voice: Notice the time of day you're in; if it's evening, on this calendar tomorrow has already begun. Think of one date that matters to you, a birthday, an anniversary, the day someone died, and wonder what it was on the moon's calendar. Just hold the idea that there's more than one way to count a life.
Luach. A tablet, and the Jewish calendar: moon months, kept in step with the sun by a leap month seven times in nineteen years.
Your line: the moon keeps time. Moon months, and a leap month to keep the seasons. Day one hundred twenty-one, done.

122.title: The new moon
122.hook: each new month is a small holiday, long honored especially by women
122.howItsDone: On Rosh Chodesh, synagogues add a short Hallel, a Torah reading and an additional service. Some women mark the day with study groups or by setting aside some work, and some communities bless the growing moon a few days later.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the luach: a calendar of moon months, with a leap month to keep the seasons. Your line was the moon keeps time.

A hilltop near Jerusalem, just after sunset, in the days the Mishnah describes. Two people squint at the western sky, looking for the thinnest sliver of moon. They see it. They hurry to the court in Jerusalem and testify. The judges question them: where was it, which way did it point? When the testimony holds, the court declares it: the new month has begun. The Mishnah says that news once traveled by torches waved from mountaintop to mountaintop, all the way to the Jews in Babylon. All that, for the first day of a month.
screen: `A SLIVER OF MOON AT SUNSET.` → `WITNESSES RUN TO THE COURT.` → `TORCHES FROM HILL TO HILL.`

segments.voice: The first day of every Jewish month has a name: Rosh Chodesh. Rosh means head; chodesh means month, from a root that means new. So the Hebrew month is named for the moon's renewal. Every month starts with a small holiday. It isn't a day off work, but the synagogue adds an extra prayer service, the psalms of praise called Hallel in a shorter form, and a special Torah reading. In the Torah, the new moons stand beside the festivals: the Book of Numbers speaks of blowing trumpets "in the day of your gladness, and in your appointed seasons, and in your new moons." In the Bible's stories, it's a day for a family meal; King Saul notices that David's seat is empty at the new moon feast. Rosh Chodesh also has a long tie to women. A midrash tells that when the people built the golden calf, the women refused to hand over their gold jewelry for it, and so they were given the new moons as a holiday of their own. Jewish law records a custom of women setting aside some work on the day. In recent decades, some Jewish women have gathered in Rosh Chodesh groups to study, sing and talk, month by month. One more custom: a few days after the new moon, as the moon grows, some Jews go outside at night and say a blessing over it. Why the moon? Because it shrinks, disappears, and comes back. The blessing over the moon makes the comparison itself: it speaks of the Jewish people as destined to be renewed like the moon.

segments.voice: Think about where the moon is right now, even if you can't see it: growing, full, shrinking, or gone dark. Then think of one part of your life that feels like the dark of the moon, something that's gone quiet. You don't have to fix it; dark is part of the cycle, not the end of it.
Rosh Chodesh. The head of the month: the new moon, kept as a small holiday, and long honored as a day for women.
Your line: renew with the moon. Every month gets its own small new beginning. Until tomorrow.

123.title: Rosh Hashanah: the shofar
123.hook: the new year opens with a ram's horn, a cry without words
123.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah, a shofar is sounded in the synagogue in patterns of tekiah, shevarim and teruah, traditionally a hundred blasts over the day, except on Shabbat. Many communities also blow it each weekday morning in the month of Elul beforehand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month, a small holiday at every new moon. Your line was renew with the moon.

Most new years begin with a countdown and a lot of noise. This one begins in a full synagogue. Someone lifts a curved animal horn to their lips, and the room goes silent. Then it comes: one long, raw, rising note. Then three broken ones, like sighing. Then a run of short, fast blasts, like sobbing. Then the long note again. No words at all. That is how Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, opens.
screen: `A NEW YEAR WITHOUT A COUNTDOWN.` → `A CURVED HORN, A SILENT ROOM.` → `A CRY WITH NO WORDS.`

segments.voice: The horn is called a shofar, usually a ram's horn, hollowed out. It's not really an instrument; it has no keys and plays no tune. The Torah never uses the name Rosh Hashanah for this day. It calls the first day of the seventh month "a day of blowing the horn unto you." That's the whole description: a day of the horn. The rabbis later named it the head of the year, and taught that on this day the whole world is judged. There are three sounds. Tekiah, one long blast. Shevarim, three broken notes. Teruah, many short staccato ones. The rabbis weren't sure exactly what the Torah's teruah sounded like, a groan or a whimper, so they kept both, and a widespread custom is to hear the sounds in many combinations, adding up to a hundred blasts over the day. The last is the tekiah gedolah, the great blast, held as long as the blower's breath will last. Why a ram's horn? It calls to mind the ram Abraham offered in place of Isaac. A cow's horn isn't used; the rabbis said it would recall the golden calf. And what does it mean? Maimonides, the medieval legal scholar and philosopher, said the shofar carries a message even though the Torah gives no reason: wake up, you sleepers, from your sleep. Look at your deeds. Come back. Others hear a coronation trumpet, or a child crying out to a parent without words. Jewish tradition holds all of these. On the Sabbath it isn't blown, and in many communities it's sounded every weekday morning in the month before, like an alarm set early.
screen: `A DAY OF BLOWING THE HORN.` · `TEKIAH, SHEVARIM, TERUAH.` · `A RAM, NOT A COW.` · `WAKE UP, YOU SLEEPERS.` · then, large: `A CRY WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Take one long breath in and let it out slowly, like a tekiah, then three broken breaths out, like shevarim. Then breathe normally and let one question sound: what have I been asleep to? A person, a habit, a feeling; there's no need to answer out loud.
Shofar. A ram's horn, blown on Rosh Hashanah in long, broken and short blasts: a cry without words that says wake up.
Your line: wake up. A cry with no words can still say it. That's day one hundred twenty-three.

124.title: Rosh Hashanah: apples, honey, water
124.hook: sweet food for a sweet year, and crumbs cast into flowing water
124.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah eve, many Jewish families eat apples dipped in honey and a round challah, often with other symbolic foods. On the first afternoon, many go to flowing water for tashlich, reading verses from Micah and sometimes tossing crumbs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shofar: a ram's horn, a cry with no words. Your line was wake up.

The shofar is serious. The table that night is sweet. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, families sit down to a round challah, the braided bread shaped into a circle for a year that comes around again. Someone passes apple slices and a small bowl of honey. You dip, and before you eat, you say a line many Jews have said for centuries: may it be God's will that this be a good and sweet year. Then the next afternoon, something stranger: whole families standing on a riverbank, turning out their pockets.
screen: `A ROUND CHALLAH.` → `APPLES DIPPED IN HONEY.` → `FAMILIES ON A RIVERBANK.`

segments.voice: Start with the table. The Talmud mentions foods eaten at the new year as good signs, things that grow quickly or come in abundance. Over time, communities built whole menus around wordplay. Pomegranates, for merits as many as their seeds. In some homes, the head of a fish, to be the head and not the tail. Dates, carrots, leeks and beets, because their Hebrew or Yiddish names sound like wishes. Apples and honey are simply the best known: sweetness, said out loud. Then comes the water. On the first afternoon of Rosh Hashanah, many Jews walk to a river, a stream, a lake or the sea, anywhere the water moves and, ideally, fish live. They read verses from the prophet Micah, which end with a picture of God's mercy: "And Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." The ceremony is named for that word, cast: tashlich, you will cast. Many bring bread crumbs and toss them in, one crumb for each thing they want to leave behind. Here's the honest part. Tashlich isn't in the Torah or the Talmud. It shows up in Germany in the late Middle Ages, and some rabbis were uneasy with it, worried people would think crumbs in a river could wash away sins by themselves. Jewish teaching is clear that they can't. The work of changing belongs to the Days of Awe, the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur. Tashlich is a picture of that work, not a substitute for it. But what a picture: you stand at moving water, and you let something go.

125.title: Yom Kippur: the fast
125.hook: twenty-five hours without food, drink or leather shoes, like angels for a day
125.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, many Jews fast for about twenty-five hours, avoid leather shoes and washing, wear white, and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer. Those whose health is at risk are required to eat, and young children do not fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tashlich: standing at moving water and letting something go. Your line was throw it in the river. On the tenth day of that same month comes Yom Kippur.

A coffee. A snack. A glass of water. A phone. A mirror. An ordinary day is full of small reaching, most of it automatic. Yom Kippur puts all of that down. No food, not even water. No leather shoes. No lotion, no washing up. From just before sunset to after nightfall the next day: about twenty-five hours. Some wear white and spend most of the day in the synagogue, standing, praying, remembering. A whole day shaped by what's set aside.
screen: `A DAY FULL OF SMALL REACHING.` → `PUT IT ALL DOWN.` → `TWENTY-FIVE HOURS.`

segments.voice: Yom Kippur means the Day of Atonement. The word kippur comes from a root often understood as covering, or wiping clean. The Torah says: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." And it gives one instruction for the body: "ye shall afflict your souls." The rabbis read that as five things to go without: eating and drinking, washing, anointing with oils, wearing leather shoes, and marital intimacy. Why leather? One explanation: leather shoes were the fine, comfortable ones, so on this day people walk a little closer to the ground. And why white? An old idea says that on Yom Kippur Jews are like angels: angels don't eat or drink, they stand, and they wear white. So for one day, people set aside the body's needs and stand like them. Two things matter as much as the fast. First, the fast is never allowed to endanger a life. Anyone who is ill, pregnant with complications, or at risk is told to eat, and Jewish law calls eating then a duty, not a failure. Young children don't fast. Second, Yom Kippur has a limit that surprises people. The Mishnah teaches that this day atones for wrongs between a person and God. For wrongs between one person and another, it doesn't, until you've gone to the person you hurt and tried to make it right. So in the days before, the custom is to call, text or knock on doors and ask: if I hurt you this year, forgive me. The hungry day in the synagogue comes after the harder conversation.

126.title: Yom Kippur: the gates close
126.hook: the day opens with Kol Nidre and ends as the gates of prayer close
126.howItsDone: Yom Kippur begins with Kol Nidre, chanted three times at sunset, and ends with Neilah, prayed standing before the open ark. It closes with the Shema, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, and a long blast of the shofar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom Kippur: twenty-five hours of fasting, standing like angels, after first making peace with the people you hurt. Your line was lighter for a day.

Yom Kippur opens with a melody and closes with a horn. At sunset, the synagogue is packed. The Torah scrolls are taken out and held, and a cantor sings a haunting old melody three times, each time a little louder: Kol Nidre. Then, a whole day later, as the light starts to fade and everyone is hungry, tired and still standing, the last prayer begins. The doors of the ark stay open. People who sat through the afternoon get to their feet. They know what time it is.
screen: `SUNSET: KOL NIDRE, THREE TIMES.` → `A WHOLE DAY OF PRAYER.` → `THE LIGHT STARTS TO FADE.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Kol Nidre means all vows. It isn't really a prayer; it's a legal formula in Aramaic, releasing the vows a person makes to God and can't keep. Jewish law is clear: it doesn't cancel promises made to other people; those have to be kept or made right with the person. Its power is the melody and the moment: a whole community admitting that people promise more than they manage. Now the end. The final service is called Neilah, which means locking, or closing. The rabbis remembered a closing prayer in the Temple, said as the great gates were locked at sunset. They also spoke of the gates of heaven, open all day to prayer, now swinging shut. So Neilah feels like the last minutes before a door closes. All through these days, the prayers have asked God to write us in the book of life. In Neilah, the word changes: seal us. The writing is almost done. Then the ending comes all at once. The congregation says the Shema, once. Then, three times, the line that follows it: blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever. Then, seven times, the words the people cried out on Mount Carmel in Elijah's day: "The LORD, He is God." And one long blast of the shofar. The fast is over. Many say next year in Jerusalem, and go home to eat. That closes a week of Modeh Ani, the calendar, the new moon, the shofar, the river, the fast, and now the gates.
